title: I have the idea need to bring it to life.
author: Useful_Use_6170
selftext: So I have an idea for creating a game, and was wondering if anyone have any tips, tools on how to slowly create this idea I have, I don’t mind keeping it 2D or using Godot, anyone that’s ever made a game would like your help what tools did you use, how can I code it without any coding knowledge and finding the assets . I was able to create it in base44 but it feels like a browser based text game.

replies.author: Useful_Use_6170
replies.body: Ummm he/she is the first artificial agent I asked. But was wondering if people who have had success making games with no codeing experience as a beginner

comments.author: Bhodar
comments.body:
I'm making a multiplayer physics-based FPS inspired by Magicka using Claude.AI.

Workflow I discovered to work for me.

Game Design Document:
Make sure you have this, with clear steps on what you want to build. What you want to include at every stage and keep it up to date and uploaded in Claude.AI's memory.

Summaries: Each session you build one or two things, create a summary of what's been made, steps included and scripts made. Upload it to Claude's Memory.

I have a working MVP after 10 sessions.

comments.author: BenTheSodaman
comments.body:
Relatively short answer for some who can get as verbose as myself, it's very possible, and it's gonna be a lot of work ahead of you the more specific your idea. 

Some of how you interacted with base44 will carry over to how you interact with Claude / Codex / Cursor, etc.

\--—- --— —-—- —-— ------- —-- -— —-—— —-—- ——— —— -——- - — -- — -- ---— -

For now, consider the 20 USD subscription of one of these services. Familiarize yourself with it a bit more. If your goal is a vertical slice to test each of your features, you may be able to accomplish that, but not too deep in anything else for 20 USD.

If you find that your usage and ideas do not exhaust your weekly limits or your monthly limit, then don't go for the 60 USD, 100 USD, or 200 USD subscriptions depending on the service you end up using. If you start to have a setup and process that can effectively utilize your subscription to most or all of its limits, then try to figure out what plan would fit you the best.

Would say not to give the agent too much to munch on all at once. There seems to be a higher rate of effing up and also burning through your tokens rapidly when that happens. Ask it to ask you what the project rules (and go to ChatGPT or Gemini to get an explanation for what some of this means, pros, and cons.)

There are going to be lots of little things we forget about or don't do, that as you put more of it together, starts to feel more "real". (e.g., scene transitions, camera zooms or pans, UI audio effects, functioning settings, graphics and coherent animations, etc.)

But all of this is just light, vague, surface-level advice from a hobbyist perspective. And as you pull the trigger to give one of these coding agents a shot or figure out how you're going to address.

replies.author: BenTheSodaman
replies.body:
Would say to think of the Cursor / Codex / etc. as a programmer who may need some guidance on what and how to code it. Out of the box, it won't know how to do a lot of things and you'll still have to lift there (e.g., the background removal of images, placing larger images or files in the correct place in the project, etc.).

\---

As an example - When I've tried to attach higher resolution images in Cursor, the file size degrades and creates issues displaying it later. e.g., a sprite sheet that's taller or wider than 1024 for example. And you may have to work around that by putting the sprite sheet directly into the location it should go.

comments.author: DamionSchubert
comments.body:
First you need to learn your tool.

Put aside your big idea.  Start small.  Ask your favorite AI agent (I like Claude) to make you a game genre that's well understood.  For example, make a match 3 game.  Then add a couple of twists to it - maybe some powerups, or some challenging goals.  Ask AI to add music and sound effects.  Mess around with every point of making a game you already know how to make work, just so you can figure out how to do it.

On one hand, it's not hard because you can talk mostly in natural language.  On the other hand, you will quickly understand the value of detailed prompts.
